I've been farming this land in Quzhou for fifty years. I know what works here and what doesn't. My land is 6 mu — I keep 4 mu in my wheat-maize rotation and 2 mu in cotton. That's what I've always done and it gives me both grain for the household and a bit of cash from the cotton.

I'm 72 now, so I'm careful about how much heavy work I take on. My wife and I manage together. I rely on my well irrigation — without it, we'd be in trouble some summers.

For the **wheat**, I plant every October. I use an improved variety I've trusted for years — better disease resistance than the old seed, and the yield is reliable. I rotary till before planting. I irrigate three times: once before winter sets in to help the roots, once at jointing, and once during grain filling. I apply fertilizer in two splits — base dressing and a top dressing at jointing. I spray for aphids and powdery mildew in spring, that's about three pesticide passes total.

For the **maize**, I go straight in after wheat harvest in June with no-tillage. I use a hybrid — Zhengdan 958 or something similar that my neighbors also use. Good ears, handles the summer heat. I only need to irrigate twice unless it's a dry year. Maize isn't as labor-heavy.

For the **cotton**, it's the hardest work — picking by hand in autumn is tough at my age — but it brings in cash. I use improved Bt cotton seed so I spray less for bollworm. I still spray five times or so across the season for other pests. Cotton needs more potassium on our soils here. I plough that field in spring before transplanting or direct seeding.
